platforms.title: Why Do Everyday Sounds Suddenly Feel Too Loud?
platforms.meta_description: Ringing in your ears, or do normal sounds suddenly feel unbearably loud? How ENT specialists tell tinnitus apart from hyperacusis, and what raises the risk.
platforms.body_html:
Hearing a ringing sound in your ears, or do sounds that never used to bother you suddenly feel loud and even painful? Ear, nose, and throat (ENT) specialists explain that tinnitus and hyperacusis come from different causes and feel different, even though they often show up together. Without telling them apart, simply pushing through can mean missing the right timing for proper management.

Why they look similar but are completely different

Tinnitus is the perception of a sound that isn't actually there — ringing, buzzing, or hissing. Common causes include inner-ear damage from noise exposure, age-related hearing loss, and side effects of certain medications. It's often more noticeable in quiet settings, and shows up even when there's no external sound at all.

Hyperacusis is an entirely different problem. It's marked by ordinary sounds that would be fine for most people feeling unusually loud or even painful. It appears to involve how the brain itself processes sound, and often follows acoustic trauma from loud noise, migraine, or jaw joint issues.

How to tell them apart, and what to check

First, whether a sound is heard with no external source at all, or whether a real, ordinary sound feels unusually painful. ENT specialists note this is the clearest distinguishing sign. Tinnitus means hearing a sound that isn't there, while hyperacusis means an actual, ordinary sound feels unbearable.

Second, whether everyday sounds are increasingly being avoided. Hyperacusis often leads to wearing earplugs constantly to avoid even ordinary noise like conversation or dishes clinking. Tinnitus is less likely to make someone avoid daily life because of the sound itself.

What matters most is not blocking out sound all day with earplugs or noise-cancelling headphones just because hyperacusis is present. Avoiding sound for too long can lead the brain to adapt toward even greater sensitivity, making symptoms worse. Working with a specialist on a gradual, guided reintroduction to sound is often part of proper management.

Treatment approaches differ too, once a diagnosis is confirmed. Tinnitus management often includes sound masking to make the phantom noise less noticeable, hearing aids if hearing loss is also present, and counseling to reduce how distressing the sound feels over time. Hyperacusis management typically centers on gradual sound therapy with an audiologist, slowly reintroducing everyday noise levels under guidance rather than avoiding them, since avoidance alone tends to make the sensitivity worse rather than better. Both conditions can improve with the right approach, but self-treating without a proper hearing evaluation risks missing an underlying cause that needs its own care.

Both risks rise with years of exposure to loud environments like construction sites or concert venues, a history of head injury, or a family history of migraine. Certain antibiotics and high-dose aspirin are also common triggers for tinnitus specifically. When it's hard to tell which one is going on, it helps to note whether a sound is heard with nothing actually there, whether an ordinary sound feels unusually painful, and whether avoidance behavior is growing. See an ENT for a hearing evaluation if either persists beyond a few weeks.

Is what you're noticing a sound with nothing actually there, or does a real, ordinary sound feel unusually painful?
